Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

REFERENCE NOTES

Mara Bell and her brother Jonah started sorting their late aunt Ruth’s photographs in February at Mara’s dining table in Albany, New York. The collection is a mixture of roughly 1,600 paper prints, about 500 scans made by Ruth, and another 300 files copied from old phones and memory cards. The estimate is not exact because some envelopes contain duplicate prints, and several memory cards have not yet been checked. Mara wrote on the first box, “We’re trying to make these findable, not solve every mystery.” They have four weekends available before Jonah’s work schedule changes in late March. Neither of them has used dedicated photo-cataloguing software before.

The paper photographs are stored in twelve shoeboxes, three albums, and a brown envelope marked “Ruth / maybe 1978.” The albums mostly cover the 1960s and 1970s, but the dates on their pages are Ruth’s handwritten captions and have not been checked against the photographs. One album has loose corners and a cracked plastic sleeve; Mara has stopped turning that page until they can lay it flat. Prints from a 1994 family reunion are mixed into a box labeled “school.” Several pictures show the same people in different seasons, and Jonah thinks two of the unknown children may be cousins, but he cannot identify them yet. A pencil note on an envelope says, “Dad’s garden, after the fence went up.” No one has established which year the fence was built.

Ruth’s scans are mostly JPEG files named with dates, such as “2001-07-04_003.jpg,” though some dates appear to come from the day Ruth scanned an older print rather than the day the picture was taken. Phone images have names like “IMG_4431.JPG” and preserve a mixture of dates and location data. Jonah has already copied the digital files to an external drive, but has not compared them with the originals or removed duplicates. The drive is currently called “Ruth stuff.” Mara has a second backup drive, which she keeps in a desk drawer in a different room. She does not want either person to rename the source files until they agree on a naming approach, because Jonah has a small script that relies on the current filenames to find matching scans.

At their first sorting session, Mara made three temporary piles: “known event,” “roughly dated,” and “not sure.” Jonah prefers not to attach a person’s name to a picture unless someone can identify that person with confidence. Their cousin Elise has offered to help identify people by video call, but she is free only on March 9 and March 16. She recognizes Ruth’s neighbors from the old block and may remember the 1988 lake trip, but she has not seen the photographs yet. Mara said, “Elise can add clues, but let’s keep who said what.” They would like a way to record a caption source or identification note without turning every uncertain guess into a confirmed fact.

1. People currently identified with confidence include Ruth Bell, Mara Bell, Jonah Bell, and their grandmother, June Bell. The family has not agreed on a standard form for names: older albums use “June,” “Grandma June,” and “J. Bell.” Mara would like the catalogue to make these references searchable together while retaining the wording written on an original caption when it matters.
2. Several recurring events are already recognizable: June’s 70th birthday in 1982, the 1988 lake trip, Jonah’s high-school graduation in 1996, and the 1994 reunion. Some photographs have no clear event or date. The family wants approximate dates to be visibly approximate, and it does not want scan dates silently treated as photo dates.
3. The collection includes pictures of addresses, car license plates, and children who are not yet identified. Mara wants those details noted only where useful for finding or handling an image, rather than copied into a public-facing description. No decision has been made to publish the catalogue, and the family has not discussed which relatives would receive access.
4. Mara is willing to scan fragile prints at home, but does not want to remove photographs from the damaged album sleeve or write directly on prints. Jonah can handle digital backups and spreadsheets; Mara can identify storage locations and type handwritten captions. Both can spend around three hours each weekend. Their aunt’s former neighbor, Mr. Dorsey, might help with the garden photographs, but they have not contacted him.
5. Jonah suggested adding a “confidence” field, while Mara suggested separate fields for the catalogue description and the original caption. They have not chosen a system or final field names. The only immediate deadline is a family lunch on March 23, when they hope to show relatives a sample of the work. If Mara and Jonah agree on the wording by October 12, Mara will print temporary box labels; if they do not agree by then, she will leave the existing box labels in place until they have reviewed the list together.

Mara has asked that the first pass remain reversible: keep original files and physical groupings identifiable, record any temporary moves, and distinguish what is visible in a picture from what someone recalls about it. Jonah’s proposed spreadsheet can be a starting point, but he has not built it yet. The 1994 reunion should not be split across folders just because some prints are currently in the “school” box. The damaged sleeve, unchecked memory cards, duplicate prints, and the uncertain garden date all remain unresolved. At the March 23 lunch, they want to show a modest sample that explains how a relative can suggest a correction without overwriting an earlier note.
